topic: NGT Clears Great Nicobar Mega Infrastructure Project

subtopics.title: Project Overview and Clearance
subtopics.summary: The Great Nicobar Mega Infrastructure Project was launched in 2021, credited to NITI Aayog, and is located on Great Nicobar Island, the southernmost island of India. The National Green Tribunal upheld its Environmental Clearance, citing compliance with Island Coastal Regulation Zone and Coastal Regulation Zone norms. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands Integrated Development Corporation is the implementing agency.
facts: Launched in 2021, credited to NITI Aayog.
Located on Great Nicobar Island, the southernmost and largest Nicobar island.
Indira Point is the southernmost point of India.
Components: International Container Transshipment Terminal, 450 MVA gas and solar-based power plant, dual-use civil-military airport, integrated township.
Strategic importance: near the Malacca Strait, vital to India's Act East Policy and QUAD Indo-Pacific Strategy.
Economic aim: cut reliance on Singapore and Colombo ports.
Implementing agency: Andaman and Nicobar Islands Integrated Development Corporation.
Covered areas include Galathea Bay, Campbell Bay and Great Nicobar, with a Biosphere Reserve and two national parks.

subtopics.title: Environmental and Tribal Concerns
subtopics.summary: The project is criticised for diverting about 130 sq. km of tropical rainforest and cutting nearly 1 million trees. The Environmental Impact Assessment used single-season data, and the proposed afforestation in Haryana cannot replicate the island's rainforest ecosystem. Tribal groups, including the Shompen and Nicobarese, face loss of habitat, cultural disruption and livelihood impact.
facts: About 130 sq. km of tropical rainforest is to be diverted.
Nearly 1 million trees are to be cut.
The Environmental Impact Assessment was based on single-season data.
Concerns exist over inadequate ecological evaluation.
Proposed afforestation in Haryana cannot replicate the tropical rainforest ecosystem.
Shompen (a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group) and the Nicobarese tribe are affected.
Concerns include loss of habitat, cultural disruption and livelihood impact.
The island lies in the highest seismic risk zone, vulnerable to earthquakes, tsunamis and climate change impacts.

subtopics.title: Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups
subtopics.summary: A Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG), previously called a Primitive Tribal Group, is a sub-classification of Scheduled Tribes that is more vulnerable than a regular Scheduled Tribe. The Dhebar Commission set up the PTG category in 1973, and the Government renamed these groups PVTGs in 2006. PM-JANMAN, with an outlay of Rs. 24,000 crore, aims to improve their socio-economic conditions.
facts: A PVTG is a sub-classification of Scheduled Tribe that is more vulnerable than a regular Scheduled Tribe.
PVTGs were previously known as Primitive Tribal Groups (PTGs).
The Dhebar Commission established the PTG category in 1973.
The Government of India renamed PTGs as PVTGs in 2006.
Salient features: technological backwardness, stagnant or declining population growth, low literacy, subsistence economy, challenging living conditions.
The Ministry of Tribal Affairs has identified 75 PVTGs across 18 states and one Union Territory.
PM-JANMAN has an outlay of Rs. 24,000 crore.
PM-JANMAN covers safe housing, clean drinking water, sanitation, health and nutrition, and road and telecom connectivity.

subtopics.title: National Green Tribunal
subtopics.summary: The National Green Tribunal is a specialised environmental tribunal set up under the National Green Tribunal Act (2010), and India is the third country after Australia and New Zealand to do so. It provides relief and compensation for environmental damage, applying the polluter pays principle and sustainable development. Its decisions can be appealed in the Supreme Court within 90 days.
facts: Set up under the National Green Tribunal Act (2010).
India is the third country, after Australia and New Zealand, to set up a specialised environmental tribunal.
Principal seat is in New Delhi; regional benches include Bhopal, Pune and Chennai.
Chairperson: a retired Supreme Court judge or High Court Chief Justice, appointed in consultation with the Chief Justice of India.
Judicial members: 10-20, exact number decided by the Central Government.
Hears civil cases under seven laws; excludes the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 and the Forest Rights Act 2006.
Appeals can be filed in the Supreme Court within 90 days.
Appeals must be disposed of within 6 months of filing.
Not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure 1908; guided by natural justice; decisions executable as a civil court decree.

quizzes.passage: The Great Nicobar Mega Infrastructure Project has returned to the spotlight after the National Green Tribunal upheld its Environmental Clearance. The Tribunal found that the project complied with the coastal norms that apply to the island. Great Nicobar is the largest island of the Nicobar group and sits at the southern end of India, where a dense green cover of trees meets long coastlines. Planners see the project as a major step in building trade and strategic capacity near the Malacca Strait. Officials argue that the plan will bring jobs, better connectivity and new economic activity to the islands. Critics, however, have questioned whether the damage to the island's fragile ecology can be offset. The island is also home to tribal communities whose way of life depends on the land and the sea. This debate highlights a familiar challenge in India: how to balance national economic and strategic goals with the protection of ecologically sensitive regions and their people. Understanding the project therefore requires knowing about the island's location, its ecology, the people who live there and the legal bodies that review such proposals. Local residents and planners will need to show how the development protects both the forest cover and the people who depend on it.

quizzes.passage: The Great Nicobar project has raised serious environmental and social concerns. Clearing large stretches of dense forest would remove habitat for wildlife and disturb an ecosystem that has developed over long periods. Critics argue that the environmental study relied on too little field data, so it may not capture how the island's species behave across changing conditions. Compensatory afforestation has been proposed in a different state, but critics say a new plantation cannot reproduce the unique structure and species of a natural forest. Indigenous communities are at the centre of the debate. Certain tribal groups are considered especially vulnerable, and they depend on the forest for food, shelter and cultural practices. Any disturbance could cause loss of habitat, disruption of traditions and a hit to local livelihoods. The island is also exposed to natural hazards. Earthquakes, tsunamis and the impacts of climate change add to concerns about building large facilities there. Supporters point to strategic and economic gains, but the debate shows how difficult it is to weigh development against ecological and tribal rights. Whether the project proceeds responsibly will depend on how well the safeguards are enforced in practice. Supporters and critics alike agree that the island's natural and human heritage needs careful protection. Clear rules on monitoring and accountability would help build trust among the communities that are most affected.
